pharm: Antisecretory / antineoplastic adjunct (growth hormone & GI hormone suppressant)
quick: Acromegaly 50 mcg SC TID initially; carcinoid 100-600 mcg/day divided
Give SC between meals and at bedtime to limit GI upset
Use only if clearly needed; limited human data
Avoid or do not breastfeed; excretion unknown
Reduce dose / extend interval in renal failure (dialysis)
Lower maintenance dose may be needed in cirrhosis
Glucose, thyroid, gallbladder USG, ECG/HR, B12
summary: Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue given by SC or IV injection that suppresses growth hormone, IGF-1, and multiple GI hormones. It controls symptoms of acromegaly, metastatic carcinoid tumors (flushing, diarrhea) and VIPomas (watery diarrhea), and is used off-label for variceal bleeding. Key risks are gallstones, glucose dysregulation and bradyarrhythmias.
indications: Acromegaly: to reduce GH and IGF-1 in patients with inadequate response to or unsuitable for surgery, irradiation and bromocriptine
Symptomatic treatment of metastatic carcinoid tumors (suppresses severe diarrhea and flushing)
Treatment of profuse watery diarrhea associated with VIP-secreting tumors (VIPomas)
Off-label: acute esophageal/gastric variceal hemorrhage; refractory diarrhea; pancreatic fistula

dosage.d: 50 mcg SC three times daily for first 2 weeks

dosage.n: Doses above 300 mcg TID rarely add benefit

dosage.d: 100-600 mcg/day SC in 2-4 divided doses for first 2 weeks
200-300 mcg/day SC in 2-4 divided doses for first 2 weeks
dosage.n: Adjust to control diarrhea; range 150-750 mcg/day

dosage.d: 50 mcg IV bolus then 50 mcg/h IV infusion

admin: Administer subcutaneously or intravenously; rotate SC injection sites systematically
Use smallest volume that delivers the dose to reduce SC injection pain; allow to reach room temperature, do not warm artificially
For IV use dilute in 50-200 mL saline or D5W and infuse over 15-30 minutes
Do NOT add to total parenteral nutrition (forms inactive glycosyl conjugate)
Give SC doses between meals and at bedtime to reduce GI side effects; inspect for particulates/discoloration
moa: Octreotide mimics natural somatostatin but is a more potent, longer-acting inhibitor of growth hormone, glucagon and insulin. It suppresses LH response to GnRH, decreases splanchnic blood flow, and inhibits release of serotonin, gastrin, VIP, secretin, motilin and pancreatic polypeptide. These actions reduce GH/IGF-1 in acromegaly and control the flushing and secretory diarrhea of carcinoid tumors and VIPomas.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to octreotide or any component of the formulation

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Human data are limited; somatostatin analogues cross the placenta. In acromegaly, fetal growth should be monitored.
lact: It is not known whether octreotide is excreted in human milk. Exercise caution; consider not breastfeeding during therapy.
renal: Clearance is reduced in renal impairment and elimination half-life is prolonged in dialysis patients; reduce maintenance dose or extend the dosing interval and titrate to response.
hepatic: Clearance is decreased in hepatic cirrhosis; the maintenance dose may need to be reduced. Monitor response carefully.

major: Bradycardic agents (beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) - additive bradycardia/AV block; dose adjustment may be needed
moderate: Insulin and oral hypoglycemics - altered glucose control; dose adjustment needed
Cyclosporine - decreased blood levels (transplant rejection risk)
Drugs largely cleared by CYP3A4 with narrow margin (e.g., quinidine) - octreotide may alter clearance
minor: Drugs with low therapeutic index requiring dose adjustment
interactions.food: Decreases intestinal absorption of dietary fat; may reduce absorption of some oral nutrients.
interactions.diagnostics: May alter thyroid function tests; can cause hypo- or hyperglycemia and Schilling test abnormalities (reduced B12).

serious: Cholelithiasis and biliary sludge with cholecystitis
Bradycardia and cardiac conduction abnormalities (AV block)

monitoring: Blood glucose (and HbA1c in diabetics); adjust antidiabetic therapy
Heart rate and ECG, especially with IV use or cardiac disease
Vitamin B12 with long-term use; GH and IGF-1 in acromegaly
counsel: Rotate injection sites and use proper aseptic SC technique
Report new abdominal pain, fatty/pale stools or yellowing of skin (gallbladder/liver)
Watch for symptoms of low or high blood sugar if diabetic
Report slow heartbeat, dizziness or fainting
Refrigerate vials; protect from light and discard unused portions
pk: GI hormone suppression within minutes (IV); rapid after SC
~0.4 h after SC (peak ~5.2 ng/mL for 100 mcg)
Up to 12 hours of GH suppression per SC dose
Refrigerate 2-8 C, protect from light; stable 14 days at room temp
pearls: Give SC doses between meals and at bedtime to minimize nausea and cramping
Baseline gallbladder ultrasound recommended; gallstones are common with chronic use
Monitor blood glucose closely - can cause both hypo- and hyperglycemia
Do not add to TPN solutions (forms inactive conjugate)
Long-acting depot (LAR) IM formulation allows monthly dosing once SC dose is stabilized
missed: For scheduled SC dosing, give the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is near the next dose, then skip it; do not double. For depot (LAR) injections, contact the prescriber to reschedule.
overdose: Reported overdoses caused transient effects such as hypo/hyperglycemia, flushing, nausea, diarrhea, weakness and bradycardia/arrhythmia. Discontinue and provide supportive symptomatic care with cardiac and glucose monitoring; no specific antidote.
